title: Development
short: Different goals, income and averages, BMI, infant mortality and HDI.
lede: Definitions plus one Indian example each — that is the answer format for the whole Economics section.
lens: **3–4 marks.** Averages (per capita income, BMI, IMR, literacy) and the limitations of income comparisons are the set questions.
The **Human Development Report** comparisons between Kerala, Haryana, Bihar and Punjab appear regularly as table-based questions.
concepts: **1. What people want from development.** Different people have different **developmental goals**. A landless rural labourer wants more days of work and better wages; a prosperous farmer of Punjab wants cheap labour and higher prices for crops; a rural woman may want the same freedom and opportunity as her brother. What may be development for one may be **destructive** for another — for example, a dam that gives electricity to industries may submerge the land of a tribal community. People also want things that money cannot buy, such as **equal treatment, freedom, security and respect**.

**2. Income and other goals.** In most cases, income is the most important component of development, because people need income to buy goods and services. But income alone cannot determine the quality of life. People look for **collective** goods too — a non-polluting environment, protection from infectious diseases, good schools and hospitals. These are available only if the community takes collective action, so development is a mix of individual and common goals.

**3. National development.** It means the improvement in the standard of living and the welfare of the people as a whole. It is decided by the **citizens' goals** taken together, so it must be fair and just. Different persons can have different notions of what is fair, and development planning has to reconcile them.

**4. Comparing states — averages.** To compare countries or states we use **averages** or per capita figures, because total income cannot be used when populations differ. **Per capita income = national income ÷ population.** According to the **World Development Report** published by the **World Bank**, countries with per capita income of **US$ 13,845 or more in 2019** are called **rich countries**, and those with per capita income of **US$ 1,045 or less** are called **low-income countries**. India comes in the category of **lower-middle-income** countries, with a per capita income of **US$ 2,110 in 2019**.

**5. Averages hide disparities.** Averages are useful for comparison but they hide differences. If the average income of a country is high, it may still be that a few people are very rich while many are extremely poor. Two states can have the same per capita income but very different **income distribution**.

concepts: **6. Kerala's example.** Kerala, with lower per capita income than Haryana, has a **lower infant mortality rate** than Haryana. The reason is the adequate provision of **basic health and educational facilities**, so that almost all children are born safe, are immunised, and are given nutrition and schooling. Health is not only the absence of disease but overall well-being, and it is not something individuals can buy — it depends on public facilities.

**7. Human Development Report.** Published by the **United Nations Development Programme (UNDP)**, the **Human Development Report** compares countries on the basis of **educational levels of the people, their health status and per capita income**. These three are combined into the **Human Development Index (HDI)**, a number between 0 and 1; the higher it is, the more developed the country. **India's HDI rank has been improving**, and countries are ranked into very high, high, medium and low human development groups. India is in the **medium human development** group.

**8. Sustainability of development.** Development should not damage the environment or exhaust resources, because resources are limited. **Groundwater** is a good example: it is an **over-exploited** resource, and in many regions of India, such as the western part of Uttar Pradesh and parts of Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana, the water table is falling. Overuse of groundwater is not sustainable, since it takes a long time to recharge. The same applies to **crude oil** — reserves will last only a limited number of years at current rates of extraction. Development must therefore be **sustainable**, using resources in a way that leaves enough for future generations.

BMI = weight in kg ÷ (height in metres)²
IMR = (infant deaths under 1 year ÷ live births) × 1,000
tricks: - **Averages are useful but hide disparities.** Every 'limitation of per capita income' answer starts with this sentence.
- **Kerala beats Haryana on health with lower income — because of public facilities.** Name health and education facilities to score.
- **HDI = health + education + income.** Three components, and the index runs 0 to 1.
mistakes: - Saying a higher BMI is always better. **Below 18.5 is undernourished, above 25 is overweight** — the healthy range is between.
- Confusing the **World Development Report** (World Bank, income-based) with the **Human Development Report** (UNDP, HDI-based).
- Using total income to compare countries. Populations differ, so **per capita** income must be used.

qa.q: Why is per capita income used to compare countries instead of total income?
qa.a: Because countries have different population sizes, so total income does not tell us what an average person earns. Dividing national income by the population gives per capita income, which shows the average income of a person and allows a fair comparison of the standard of living between countries.

qa.q: Kerala has a lower per capita income than Haryana but a lower infant mortality rate. Explain.
qa.a: Because Kerala has an adequate provision of basic health and educational facilities. Almost all children are born safe, are immunised and are given nutrition, and the literacy rate is high, so mothers are better able to care for their children. These facilities are public goods that individuals cannot buy, so a higher income alone does not reduce the infant mortality rate.

qa.q: What is the Human Development Report and on what basis does it compare countries?
a: It is published every year by the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). It compares countries on the basis of three things: the **educational levels of the people**, their **health status**, and their **per capita income**.

These three are combined into the **Human Development Index (HDI)**, a figure between 0 and 1; the closer to 1, the higher the level of human development. Countries are grouped as having very high, high, medium or low human development.

The report is important because it recognises that income alone does not measure development — a country may be rich but have poor health and education, in which case its people are not truly developed. India has been improving its rank and is placed in the medium human development group.

qa.q: Explain the term sustainability of development with reference to groundwater.
qa.a: Sustainability of development means using resources in a way that meets present needs without exhausting them, so that future generations can meet their own needs. Groundwater is a renewable resource but it is being over-exploited in many parts of India, such as western Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Punjab and Haryana, where the water table is falling. Since it takes a long time to recharge, continued overuse is not sustainable and will leave future generations without water.

qa.q: Why do different people have different notions of development?
qa.a: Because their life situations are different. A landless rural labourer wants more days of work and better wages, a prosperous farmer wants higher prices for his crops and cheap labour, an industrialist wants more electricity and better roads, and a tribal community wants its forest and land protected. What is development for one person may be destructive for another, so development goals are always contested.

title: Sectors of the Indian Economy
short: Primary, secondary, tertiary; organised and unorganised; GDP.
lede: Six classifications of economic activity. Learn one example for each and every question on this chapter is answerable.
lens: **3–5 marks.** The difference between organised and unorganised sectors, and disguised unemployment with rural labourers, are the set questions.

Table-based questions on the share of GDP and of employment by sector appear often — learn that the **tertiary sector produces the largest share of GDP but the primary sector still employs the most people**.
concepts: **1. Sectors of economic activity.** **Primary** — activities that use natural resources directly: agriculture, dairy, fishing, forestry, mining. **Secondary** — activities in which natural products are changed into other forms through manufacturing: turning sugarcane into sugar, cotton into cloth, or iron ore into steel. **Tertiary** — activities that **support** the primary and secondary sectors instead of producing goods: transport, banking, communication, trade, education, health, insurance, and information technology. The tertiary sector is also called the **service sector**.

**2. Why the tertiary sector is growing.** As income rises, people demand more services such as eating out, tourism, shopping and private hospitals. Basic services such as hospitals, schools, postal and communication services are required by the government and by every citizen. The development of agriculture and industry has led to the development of services such as transport and trade. New services based on **information and communication technology** have become essential. As a result, in India the tertiary sector has emerged as the **largest producing sector**, replacing the primary sector, and it now contributes the largest share to GDP.

**3. Employment in the sectors.** Although the tertiary sector produces the largest share of GDP, **the primary sector still employs the largest number of people in India** — more than half the workforce. This means that the growth of the service sector has not generated enough employment for everyone.

**4. Disguised unemployment and underemployment.** **Underemployment** means people are working less than what they are capable of and willing to do. In agriculture, a family of five may all work on a small plot although three would be enough — if the extra members are withdrawn, production does not fall. This is **disguised unemployment**, also called **hidden unemployment**. In urban areas, casual workers such as painters, plumbers and repair persons work only when they get work. Underemployment is also seen where highly educated people work as clerks or labourers. **Remedy:** in rural areas, more irrigation facilities, credit and cheap inputs would raise agricultural output and create work; **construction** such as dams, canals and roads would create employment; and in urban areas, more industries and service enterprises could absorb the surplus labour. The **Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 (MGNREGA)** guarantees **100 days of wage employment in a year** to every rural household whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual work, and gives a legally guaranteed right to work.

**5. Organised and unorganised sectors.** The **organised sector** has enterprises registered with the government, which follow rules on working conditions, hours, overtime, leave and holidays; workers get **job security, paid leave, provident fund, medical benefits and other facilities** protected by law, and are covered by the **Factories Act** and other labour laws. The **unorganised sector** has small, scattered units largely outside government control; jobs are low-paid, irregular and insecure, with no paid leave, no provident fund and no job security. Most workers in the unorganised sector are small farmers, landless labourers, artisans, street vendors and construction workers. About **90% of workers in India are in the unorganised sector**. They need protection on three issues: **wages**, **safety at work**, and **social security** such as health and old-age support.

**6. Public and private sectors.** The **public sector** is owned by the government and works with the objective of **public welfare** rather than profit — railways, posts, NTPC, ONGC, SAIL. It provides essential services at reasonable rates, cares for the welfare of the poor, and supports areas where private enterprise will not invest. The **private sector** is owned by individuals or companies and works for **profit** — TISCO, Reliance, Infosys.

**7. Gross Domestic Product (GDP).** The total value of all **final goods and services** produced within a country during a particular year is called GDP. Only **final goods** are counted, to avoid **double counting** — the value of the wheat is included in the value of the flour, and that in the value of the bread. The production of each sector is estimated by the concerned ministry and department, and the **Central Statistics Office** collects the data. GDP is measured for the whole country and is divided into the contribution of the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors.

**8. National Rural Employment Guarantee and the shift in the economy.** The rise of the tertiary sector and the fall of agriculture's share in GDP is a feature of **economic development** — in developed countries the service sector dominates. But employment has not shifted at the same rate, so India has a large workforce still dependent on agriculture with low incomes, which is why MGNREGA and rural development matter.
tricks: - **Primary = extract, Secondary = make, Tertiary = support.** One word each.
- **The paradox to remember:** tertiary produces the most GDP, primary employs the most people.
- **Disguised unemployment = extra people, same output.** The test question is 'if some are withdrawn, does production fall?'
mistakes: - Counting intermediate goods in GDP. Only **final goods** are counted, to avoid double counting.
- Saying the tertiary sector employs the largest number of people in India. It produces the largest share of GDP, but the **primary sector** employs the most.
- Forgetting that MGNREGA guarantees **100 days**, not 200.

qa.q: Distinguish between the primary, secondary and tertiary sectors with one example of each.
qa.a: The primary sector includes activities that use natural resources directly, such as agriculture, dairy, fishing and mining. The secondary sector includes activities in which natural products are changed into other forms through manufacturing, such as turning sugarcane into sugar or cotton into cloth. The tertiary sector includes activities that support the primary and secondary sectors without producing goods, such as transport, banking, trade, education and health.

qa.q: What is disguised unemployment? Give an example from rural India.
qa.a: Disguised or hidden unemployment is a situation in which more people are employed in a job than are actually required, so that withdrawing some of them does not reduce production. In rural India, a family of five may all work on a small plot of land although three would be enough; if the extra two members leave, output does not fall. They appear employed but are in fact surplus.

qa.q: Compare the working conditions in the organised and unorganised sectors.
a: **Organised sector:** enterprises are registered with the government and must follow rules on working hours, overtime, leave and holidays. Workers get regular employment, job security, paid leave, provident fund, medical benefits and other facilities, and are protected by laws such as the Factories Act and the Minimum Wages Act.

**Unorganised sector:** small, scattered units largely outside government control. Work is irregular and low paid, there is no job security, no paid leave, no provident fund and no medical benefits, and working conditions are often unsafe.
**Scale:** about 90% of the workers in India are in the unorganised sector — small farmers, landless labourers, artisans, street vendors, construction workers and domestic workers.
**What is needed:** protection of wages, safety at the workplace, and social security such as health cover and old-age support.

qa.q: Why has the tertiary sector become the most important sector in India? Give five reasons.
a: **Basic services:** services such as hospitals, educational institutions, postal and telegraph services, police stations, courts, banks and insurance companies are required by every citizen and by the government, and their expansion is essential for development.
**Growing demand with rising income:** as incomes rise, people demand more services such as eating out, tourism, shopping, private hospitals and private schools.
**Support to agriculture and industry:** the development of the primary and secondary sectors has led to the development of services such as transport, storage and trade.
**New services:** information and communication technology has made new services essential, and India has become a major provider of software and business process services.
**Employment and GDP:** the sector now contributes the largest share of GDP and has created a wide range of jobs, from call centres to consultancy, making it the largest producing sector in India.

qa.q: What is GDP and why are only final goods counted in it?
qa.a: Gross Domestic Product is the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country during a particular year. Only final goods are counted because the value of intermediate goods is already included in the value of the final product — the value of wheat is included in the flour, and of the flour in the bread. Counting both would amount to double counting.

qa.q: What is MGNREGA 2005 and how does it help to reduce unemployment?
qa.a: The Mahatma Gandhi National Rural Employment Guarantee Act 2005 guarantees 100 days of wage employment in a year to every rural household whose adult members volunteer to do unskilled manual work. If the government fails to provide work within fifteen days, the applicant is entitled to an unemployment allowance. It creates a legal right to work, raises rural incomes, and builds rural assets such as ponds, roads and irrigation channels.

title: Money and Credit
short: Modern money, banks, credit terms, SHGs and debt traps.
lede: Credit is a double-edged sword — that sentence is the whole chapter, and most of the marks.
lens: **3–4 marks.** The role of banks as mediators, the difference between formal and informal credit, and self-help groups are the set questions.
Case-based questions describe a farmer borrowing from a moneylender and ask you to identify the problem and the better alternative.
concepts: **1. Money as a medium of exchange.** Before money, exchange took place through the **barter system**, which required a **double coincidence of wants** — each party had to want what the other offered. Money solves this problem because it acts as an **intermediate step** in exchange, and is therefore called a **medium of exchange**. **Modern money** is currency, which is accepted as a medium of exchange not because it is useful in itself or made of precious metal, but because it is **authorised by the government**. The **Reserve Bank of India** issues currency notes on behalf of the Central Government; no other individual or organisation is allowed to issue currency. The RBI also supervises the functioning of banks, ensures that banks maintain a minimum cash balance and lend to small borrowers as well as big ones, and monitors that banks submit information on lending.

**2. Loan activities of banks.** Banks keep a small proportion of deposits as **cash** (about 15% in India) to pay depositors who may come to withdraw on any day, and use the major portion to extend **loans**. In return, banks pay **interest on deposits** and charge a **higher interest on loans**; the difference between what is charged from borrowers and what is paid to depositors is the bank's main source of income. Banks thus act as **mediators** between those who have surplus money and those who need it.

head: Term
Meaning
rows: an asset owned by the borrower (land, vehicle, livestock, deposits) used as a guarantee until the loan is repaid
an agreement in which the lender supplies money, goods or services with the promise of future repayment
the percentage of the principal charged for the use of money
a situation where the borrower cannot repay and has to take another loan, so debt keeps growing
loans from banks and cooperatives, supervised by the RBI, at low and fair rates
loans from moneylenders, traders, friends and relatives, at high rates, with no supervision

concepts: **3. Two different credit situations.** **Salim**, a shoe manufacturer in Delhi, took a loan from a trader, completed the order and repaid the loan with profit — here **credit played a vital and positive role**. **Swapna**, a small farmer in Andhra Pradesh, borrowed from a moneylender at a high rate to grow groundnut; the crop failed, and to repay the earlier loan she had to take another, and eventually had to sell part of her land — here **credit pushed her into a debt trap**. So credit can either help or harm, depending on the situation, the risk and the support available.

**4. Formal sector credit in India.** **Banks and cooperatives** are the main sources of formal credit. **Cooperative societies** pool the resources of their members, accept deposits and lend to members at a low rate of interest; they are supervised by the RBI. But formal credit reaches only a small part of rural India: in **urban areas about 85% of poor households borrow from informal sources**, and in **rural areas about 70%** do. Only about **half of the total poor households in India borrow mostly from informal sources** — moneylenders, traders, employers, relatives and friends. Why the imbalance: banks and cooperatives require **collateral** and documentation, which poor households do not have; banks are not present everywhere in rural India; and small borrowers are considered risky. The result is that informal lenders charge **much higher interest**, and the high cost of borrowing means that a large part of the borrower's earnings goes to repayment, so the debt grows.

**5. Self-help groups.** A **self-help group (SHG)** is a group of 15–20 members, usually women from one neighbourhood, who meet and save regularly, each contributing **₹ 25 to ₹ 100 or more** per saving session. Members can take **small loans from the group itself** at a low rate of interest. After a year or two of regular savings, the group becomes eligible for a **loan from a bank**, which is sanctioned in the name of the group, with the group itself responsible for repayment. By 2017–18, more than **9 crore women** were members of SHGs. **Grameen Bank of Bangladesh**, started by **Muhammad Yunus** in the 1970s, showed that poor women can repay loans reliably; it grew to over 9 million members. SHGs help borrowers overcome the problem of lack of collateral, provide a platform to discuss social issues such as health, nutrition and domestic violence, and make women financially self-reliant.

**6. Why credit should be available to all.** Cheap and affordable credit is essential for a country's development, because farmers need loans for seeds, fertilisers and equipment, and small entrepreneurs need loans to start or expand enterprises. At present most of the credit is available only to the rich, so the government should encourage formal sources of lending, expand banks and cooperatives into rural areas, and ensure that small borrowers get loans at a reasonable rate. This is the role of the RBI's supervision and of SHGs.
tricks: - **Credit helps Salim and traps Swapna.** Name both in any credit question and you have the whole argument.
- **Formal = banks and cooperatives (RBI supervised, low rates, collateral needed). Informal = moneylenders (high rates, no supervision, no collateral).**
- **SHG = 15–20 women, save ₹25–100, lend internally, then bank loan to the group.** Those four facts cover the question.
mistakes: - Saying currency is accepted because it has intrinsic value. It is accepted because it is **authorised by the government**, and issued by the RBI.
- Attributing Grameen Bank to India. It is in **Bangladesh**, founded by **Muhammad Yunus**.
- Writing that SHG members borrow individually from the bank. The loan is sanctioned **in the name of the group**.

qa.q: Why is money called a medium of exchange?
qa.a: Because it acts as an intermediate step in the exchange of goods and services. In a barter system, exchange requires a double coincidence of wants — each person must want what the other has. Money removes this difficulty: a person can sell his goods for money and use that money to buy whatever he wants, so it mediates between the two parties.

qa.q: What is collateral and why do banks ask for it?
qa.a: Collateral is an asset that the borrower owns — such as land, a building, a vehicle, livestock or deposits with banks — and uses as a guarantee to a lender until the loan is repaid. Banks ask for it so that if the borrower fails to repay, the bank can sell the asset to recover its money. Because poor households often have no collateral, they are excluded from formal credit.

qa.q: Explain with an example how credit can either help or harm the borrower.
a: **Where credit helps — Salim:** Salim, a shoe manufacturer in Delhi, received a large order for 30,000 pairs of shoes to be delivered within a month. He took a loan from a trader, bought the raw material, completed the order on time, made a profit and repaid the loan. Here credit enabled him to expand production and earn more.

**Where credit harms — Swapna:** Swapna, a small farmer in Andhra Pradesh, borrowed ₹ 2,500 from a moneylender at a high rate of interest to cultivate groundnut. The crop failed because of pest attack, and to repay the first loan she had to take another. Over three years her debt grew, and she finally had to sell a part of her land to repay the loan. This is a **debt trap** — a situation where credit pushes the borrower into a cycle from which she cannot escape.

**Conclusion:** whether credit improves a person's situation depends on the risk involved and on whether there is support if something goes wrong. Credit is therefore essential but must be available on fair terms.

qa.q: What are self-help groups and how do they help poor borrowers?
a: A self-help group is a group of about 15–20 members, usually women belonging to one neighbourhood, who meet regularly and save, each contributing anything from ₹ 25 to ₹ 100 or more.
**Internal lending:** members can take small loans from the group itself, at a rate of interest decided by the group but lower than that charged by moneylenders.

**Bank loans:** after a year or two of regular savings, the group becomes eligible for a loan from a bank. The loan is sanctioned in the name of the group, and the group is responsible for repayment, so members keep track of each other's borrowing.

**Why it helps:** it overcomes the problem of lack of collateral, provides credit at a reasonable rate, makes women financially self-reliant, and creates a platform for women to discuss health, nutrition, domestic violence and education. The Grameen Bank of Bangladesh, started by Muhammad Yunus, demonstrated that poor women are reliable borrowers; today more than 9 crore women in India belong to self-help groups.

qa.q: Why do most poor households in India still depend on informal sources of credit?
qa.a: Because banks and cooperatives demand collateral and documentation which poor households do not possess, banks are not present in all rural areas, and small borrowers are treated as risky. Moneylenders and traders, by contrast, lend without collateral and are available in the village, even though they charge much higher rates of interest.

qa.q: What is the role of the Reserve Bank of India in supervising banks?
qa.a: The RBI supervises the functioning of formal sources of loans. It ensures that banks maintain a minimum cash balance, that they lend not just to profit-making businesses but also to small cultivators, small-scale industries and small borrowers, and that they submit periodical information to the RBI on how much they are lending, to whom and at what interest rate.

title: Globalisation and the Indian Economy
short: MNCs, foreign trade, liberalisation, WTO and fair globalisation.
lede: One story: how production, trade and investment crossed borders, and what India did about it in 1991.
lens: **3–5 marks.** MNCs and how they control production, and liberalisation with its effects on workers and small producers, are the set questions.
The terms **WTO, MNC, liberalisation and special economic zones** must be defined precisely — definitions carry marks here.
concepts: **1. What is globalisation?** The integration of the economies of various countries of the world through the free movement of goods, services, capital and technology, and the free movement of labour. It is the result of a long historical process, but it has accelerated in the last three decades. Its two main features are the **interconnection** of production and markets across countries, and the **integration** of markets so that the price of a product tends to become the same everywhere.

**2. Production across countries — MNCs.** A **multinational corporation (MNC)** is a corporation that owns or controls production of goods or services in **two or more countries other than its home country**. It sets up offices and factories for production in regions where it can get **cheap labour, resources and other factors**, and keeps the **large profits with itself**. MNCs control production in three ways: **setting up new factories** in the host country (which creates employment); **buying or acquiring a local company** and expanding it, which is the quickest way and is possible because foreign investment rules have been eased — **Ford Motors** acquired a stake in Mahindra; and **placing orders with small producers** — garments, footwear and sports items — which are then sold under the MNC's brand name. The third route lets the MNC control small producers without owning them: it sets the **price, quality, delivery and labour conditions**.

**3. Foreign trade and integration of markets.** Foreign trade creates an opportunity for producers to reach beyond the domestic market, so they can sell in markets abroad and buyers can choose between products produced in different countries. Integration happens when **prices of similar products in two markets tend to become the same**, producers in the two countries become close competitors, and even when protected by import barriers, foreign producers enter and change the domestic market. **Example:** in India, after the 1990s, the number of car models rose sharply, and buyers got a much wider choice because of foreign trade and foreign investment.

**4. Liberalisation in India (1991).** **Liberalisation** means removing barriers or restrictions set by the government on what can be imported or exported, and on foreign investment. Until 1991, India protected domestic producers because many industries were just coming up in the 1950s and 1960s and would not have been able to compete with foreign imports. In **1991** the government decided that Indian producers had to improve their quality and compete internationally, and that **foreign competition would improve the performance of producers in India**. So import barriers were reduced, and decisions about what to import or export, and how much, were left to individual producers and buyers. **Foreign investment rules were also liberalised**, and organisations such as the **WTO** pushed for this. **Flexibility in labour laws** was also introduced, allowing companies to employ workers on a contract basis for short periods, which reduced job security.

**5. The World Trade Organization (WTO).** Started in **1995** at the insistence of developed countries, the WTO sets the rules for international trade and ensures that member countries follow them. Its aim is to liberalise international trade and to remove barriers. It has about **164 member countries**, and all decisions are taken by consensus among members. The criticism is that the rules are often **biased in favour of developed countries**, and that developing countries have had to remove trade barriers while developed ones continue to protect their own agriculture — for example the USA supporting its farmers while pressing India to remove agricultural subsidies.

**6. Impact of globalisation on India.** **Positive:** MNCs have increased investment in India — **Ford, Samsung, Hyundai, Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Nokia** and others have set up production; Indian companies such as **Tata Motors, Infosys, Ranbaxy, Sundaram Fasteners** have themselves become multinationals by acquiring foreign companies; consumers have greater choice at lower prices and better quality; top Indian companies have benefited from competition and now compete globally; **IT and services** have grown rapidly, with business process outsourcing employing lakhs; and India receives a large part of the world's **remittances** from Indians working abroad. **Negative:** globalisation has hit **small producers and workers** hardest. Small industries making batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products, vegetable oil, groundnut oil and **matchboxes** could not compete with cheap imports and many units were shut down, leaving workers unemployed. Workers are increasingly employed on **temporary contracts** at low wages with no job security, and small farmers have been affected by cheap agricultural imports.

**7. Special Economic Zones and fair globalisation.** **Special Economic Zones (SEZs)** are industrial areas set up by the government with world-class facilities — electricity, water, roads, transport, storage, recreational and educational facilities — where companies that set up production get **tax exemption for five years**. SEZs are at **Noida, Gandhidham, Falta, Cochin, Chennai, Visakhapatnam, Santacruz, Kandla, Surat, Nellore** and elsewhere. **Fair globalisation** would create opportunities for all and ensure that the benefits of globalisation are shared better. For this the government must support small producers to improve their performance until they become strong enough to compete, protect workers' rights and implement labour laws properly, negotiate for fairer rules at the WTO, and align with other developing countries. **People's movements** and workers' organisations also play a role in ensuring that globalisation is fair.
tricks: - **MNC = production in two or more countries besides the home country.** That exact wording is a marked step.
- **Three ways MNCs control production: build, buy, place orders.** 'Build, buy, brand.'
- **1991 = liberalisation; 1995 = WTO.** Two dates, no ambiguity.
mistakes: - Saying liberalisation removes all government control. It removes **barriers on trade and foreign investment**, not all regulation.
- Describing the WTO as an Indian institution or giving its start date as 1991. It began in **1995**.
- Attributing the growth of SEZs to private initiative alone. They are **set up by the government** with world-class facilities.

qa.q: What is a multinational corporation? How do MNCs spread their production?
qa.a: A multinational corporation is a corporation that owns or controls production of goods or services in two or more countries other than its home country. MNCs set up factories in regions where they can get cheap labour, resources and other factors of production, and they keep the large profits with themselves. They spread production by setting up new factories, by buying or acquiring a local company and expanding it, or by placing orders with small producers which are then sold under the MNC's brand name.

qa.q: What is liberalisation and why did the Indian government introduce it in 1991?
qa.a: Liberalisation means removing barriers or restrictions set by the government on trade and on foreign investment. The government introduced it in 1991 because it felt that Indian producers needed to improve the quality of what they produced, and that foreign competition would improve the performance of producers in India, since they would have to improve quality to compete with imports.

qa.q: How has globalisation affected small producers and workers in India?
a: **Small producers:** many small industries producing items such as batteries, capacitors, plastics, toys, tyres, dairy products, vegetable oil, groundnut oil and matchboxes could not compete with cheap imports and had to shut down, leaving lakhs of workers unemployed. Small farmers have also been affected by cheap agricultural imports from developed countries.

**Workers:** globalisation has brought pressure on employers to be 'flexible', so workers are increasingly hired on **temporary contracts** for short periods, with low wages, long hours and no job security or benefits such as provident fund and medical cover. Labour laws are often not implemented.
**The result:** globalisation has made the rich richer and has increased the insecurity of the poor, so many workers' organisations and people's movements have been demanding fairer rules.
**But:** in some sectors, such as information technology and services, globalisation has created new employment opportunities, and consumers have benefited from lower prices and wider choice.

qa.q: What is the WTO and what criticism is made of it?
a: The World Trade Organization was started in **1995** at the insistence of developed countries. It sets the rules for international trade, and all decisions are taken by consensus among its member countries, of which there are about 164.
**Aim:** to liberalise international trade, and to ensure that countries remove trade barriers such as taxes on imports, since it is believed that this will allow countries to specialise and grow.

**Criticism:** the rules of the WTO are often biased in favour of developed countries. Developed countries have kept some trade barriers, particularly in agriculture, and have supported their own farmers with subsidies, while asking developing countries to remove their barriers. Developing countries have had to comply with WTO rules, but the benefits have not been shared equally. Hence the demand for **fair globalisation**.

qa.q: What are Special Economic Zones and what facilities do they offer?
qa.a: Special Economic Zones are industrial areas set up by the government with world-class facilities such as electricity, water, roads, transport, storage, recreational and educational facilities. Companies that set up production in an SEZ do not have to pay tax for an initial period of five years, and labour laws are applied flexibly. SEZs are located at places such as Noida, Gandhidham, Falta, Cochin, Chennai and Kandla, with the aim of attracting foreign investment.

qa.q: What is fair globalisation and how can it be achieved?
qa.a: Fair globalisation would create opportunities for all and ensure that the benefits of globalisation are shared better, rather than concentrating them in the hands of the rich. It can be achieved by the government supporting small producers with credit, technology and training until they are strong enough to compete, by implementing labour laws properly and protecting workers' rights, by negotiating with other developing countries at the WTO for fairer rules, and by supporting people's movements that campaign against unfair trade rules.

title: Consumer Rights
short: Exploitation in the marketplace, COPRA, consumer groups and duties.
lede: Assessed mainly as project work, but the rights, COPRA and the redressal machinery still appear as short questions.
lens: **Project work in the internal assessment** — the usual project is a survey of a local shop, a study of ISI and Agmark labels, or a consumer-court case write-up.
As a theory question it appears as a 3-marker on the consumer's rights or on the redressal machinery under COPRA.
concepts: **1. The consumer in the marketplace.** A consumer is a person who buys goods and services for personal use. In the marketplace, consumers are often **exploited**: shopkeepers may give less weight than they claim, sell adulterated or defective goods, add hidden charges, or refuse to give a bill so that there is no proof of purchase. **Producers and traders** are far fewer in number, better organised and more powerful than consumers, who are scattered and buy in small quantities. **False advertising** and the sale of goods that do not meet safety standards are other common problems.

**2. Why consumers must be aware.** Awareness is the first step. A consumer should check the **MRP**, the **expiry date**, the **date of manufacture**, the **batch number**, the **net quantity**, and the **ISI, Agmark or Hallmark** certification marks where relevant. The consumer should insist on a **cash memo** (bill), because it is proof of purchase and is needed to file a complaint. Consumers should also know their rights and the process of redressal.

**3. The consumer movement in India.** It arose out of dissatisfaction with the many unfair practices of sellers, and because there was no legal system to protect consumers from exploitation in the marketplace. Until the 1960s, consumer organisations were mostly writing articles and holding exhibitions. The movement gained force after the **1980s**, when issues such as food adulteration, hoarding, black marketing and shortage of goods were raised. In **1986** the Indian Parliament enacted the **Consumer Protection Act (COPRA)**, which recognises consumers' rights and sets up the machinery for redressal. A major step was the right to seek redressal against unfair trade practices and exploitation. India also observes **24 December as National Consumers' Day**, because the Act was enacted on that day in 1986.

**4. Consumer rights.** (a) **Right to be informed** — the right to know about the quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price of goods, so that the consumer is protected against unfair trade practices. This is why the government made it mandatory to print the MRP, expiry date and ingredients. (b) **Right to choose** — the right to be assured of access to a variety of goods and services at competitive prices. (c) **Right to seek redressal** — the right to seek remedy against unfair trade practices or exploitation, and to be compensated. (d) **Right to represent** — the right to be heard and to represent oneself in the consumer courts. (e) **Right to safety** — protection against goods that are hazardous to life and health. (f) **Right to consumer education.**

**5. The redressal machinery under COPRA.** A **three-tier quasi-judicial machinery** was set up: the **District Commission** (formerly District Forum) for claims up to a specified value, the **State Commission** for higher claims, and the **National Commission** at the top. A consumer aggrieved by the order of a District or State Commission can appeal to the higher level. The process: the consumer files a complaint with a copy of the bill and other proof; if the court finds the case genuine, it may direct the trader to remove the defect, replace the goods, refund the price, pay compensation for loss or injury, or discontinue the unfair practice.

**6. Consumer organisations.** **Consumer protection councils**, **consumer groups**, **women's organisations** and **residents' welfare associations** play a major role in spreading awareness, helping consumers file cases, and pressuring traders and the government. **Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS)** certifies goods with the **ISI mark**; **Agmark** certifies agricultural produce; the **Hallmark** certifies the purity of gold and silver. **Legal Metrology** ensures correct weights and measures. **RTI (Right to Information) Act 2005** also empowers consumers to ask government departments about their functioning.

**7. Duties of a consumer.** Check the expiry and manufacturing dates and the certification marks; ask for a bill; do not buy adulterated or defective goods; complain when cheated, since silence encourages the trader; form consumer groups; and buy only standardised goods where certification is available.
tricks: - **COPRA 1986, enacted on 24 December = National Consumers' Day.** The date and the Act go together.
- **Six rights: informed, choose, redressal, represent, safety, education.** *'I Choose Redressal, Representation, Safety, Education'.*
- **Three-tier machinery: District, State, National Commission.** Always in that order.
mistakes: - Calling the district level a 'District Forum'. Under the present Act it is the **District Commission**.
- Saying a consumer can go straight to the National Commission. Appeals go **district → state → national**.
- Confusing **ISI** (industrial goods, Bureau of Indian Standards) with **Agmark** (agricultural produce).

qa.q: Explain any three rights of a consumer.
qa.a: **Right to be informed:** the right to know about the quality, quantity, purity, standard and price of goods so as to be protected against unfair trade practices; this is why the MRP, expiry date and ingredients must be printed on packets. **Right to choose:** the right to be assured of access to a variety of goods and services at competitive prices. **Right to seek redressal:** the right to seek remedy against unfair trade practices or exploitation, and to be compensated for loss or injury.

qa.q: What is COPRA and what machinery did it set up?
qa.a: COPRA is the Consumer Protection Act, enacted by the Indian Parliament in 1986, which recognises the rights of consumers and provides machinery for redressal. It set up a three-tier quasi-judicial machinery — the District Commission, the State Commission and the National Commission — before which a consumer can file a complaint along with proof of purchase.

qa.q: Why is the consumer often exploited in the marketplace and how can this be overcome?
a: **Why:** traders and producers are few in number, well organised and powerful, while consumers are scattered and buy in small quantities, so they cannot bargain effectively. Sellers give less weight, sell adulterated or defective goods, add hidden charges, and refuse to give bills so that there is no proof of purchase. False advertising and unsafe goods add to the problem.

**How it can be overcome:** (1) the consumer must be **aware** — check the MRP, expiry and manufacture dates, batch number, net quantity and the ISI, Agmark or Hallmark marks; (2) always insist on a **cash memo**, since it is the proof of purchase needed to file a complaint; (3) know and use the **consumer's rights**, including the right to seek redressal before the District, State or National Commission; (4) form and support **consumer groups** and organisations, which have been instrumental in spreading awareness and pressuring traders and the government; (5) use the **RTI Act** to obtain information from government departments; and (6) the government must enforce standards and penalise unfair trade practices.

qa.q: What is the significance of 24 December in the context of consumer rights in India?
qa.a: It is observed as National Consumers' Day in India because the Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (COPRA) was enacted by Parliament on 24 December 1986. The day is used to spread awareness about consumer rights and the machinery available for redressal.

qa.q: What are the duties of a consumer?
qa.a: A consumer should check the expiry and manufacturing dates and the certification marks such as ISI, Agmark and Hallmark; ask for a bill as proof of purchase; avoid adulterated or defective goods and report them; complain to the trader or to the consumer commission when cheated instead of remaining silent; join or form consumer groups; and prefer standardised goods where certification is available.

qa.q: Discuss “Consumer Rights” in detail. Include the idea that carries marks, one worked example or answer frame, and why students lose marks.
a: The consumer in the marketplace. A consumer is a person who buys goods and services for personal use. In the marketplace, consumers are often exploited: shopkeepers may give less weight than they claim, sell adulterated or defective goods, add hidden charges, or refuse to give a bill so that there is no proof of purchase. Producers and traders are far fewer in number, better organised and more powerful than consumers.
Marks lens: Project work in the internal assessment — the usual project is a survey of a local shop, a study of ISI and Agmark labels, or a consumer-court case write-up.
Method / memory trick: COPRA 1986, enacted on 24 December = National Consumers' Day. The date and the Act go together.
Do not: Calling the district level a 'District Forum'. Under the present Act it is the District Commission.

qa.q: Riya is revising “Consumer Rights” (Exploitation in the marketplace, COPRA, consumer groups and duties.). A classmate lost marks by doing this: Calling the district level a 'District Forum'. Under the present Act it is the District Commission. Apply the correct method and rewrite the scoring answer.
a: Correct method: COPRA 1986, enacted on 24 December = National Consumers' Day. The date and the Act go together.
Why the mistake costs marks: Calling the district level a 'District Forum'. Under the present Act it is the District Commission.

qa.q: Amit is given this exam-style task from “Consumer Rights”: “Explain any three rights of a consumer.” Treat it as an application question. Identify the idea, then write the working in points.
a: Idea: Exploitation in the marketplace, COPRA, consumer groups and duties..

Right to be informed: the right to know about the quality, quantity, purity, standard and price of goods so as to be protected against unfair trade practices; this is why the MRP, expiry date and ingredients must be printed on packets. Right to choose: the right to be assured of access to a variety of goods and services at competitive prices. Right to seek redressal: the right to seek remedy against unfair trade practices or exploitation, and to be compensated for loss or injury.

mcq.q: The Consumer Protection Act (COPRA) was enacted in India in: (a) 1980 (b) 1986 (c) 1991 (d) 2005
mcq.a: **(b) 1986**, on 24 December, which is observed as National Consumers' Day.

mcq.q: The certification mark for the purity of gold is: (a) ISI (b) Agmark (c) Hallmark (d) FPO
mcq.a: **(c) Hallmark.** ISI is for industrial goods and Agmark for agricultural produce.

mcq.q: A consumer dissatisfied with the order of the District Commission can appeal to: (a) the National Commission directly (b) the State Commission (c) the High Court only (d) the District Magistrate
mcq.a: **(b) the State Commission** — the appeal moves district → state → national.

mcq.q: The most exam-ready way to revise “Consumer Rights” is: (a) read the heading only  (b) learn the key idea plus one example  (c) skip written practice  (d) memorise a random extra topic
mcq.a: **(b) learn the key idea plus one example.** The chapter is Exploitation in the marketplace, COPRA, consumer groups and duties..

mcq.q: A 3-mark answer on “Consumer Rights” should: (a) be one sentence  (b) start with the idea, then a reason or method  (c) copy the whole chapter  (d) leave the example out
mcq.a: **(b) start with the idea, then a reason or method.** Step marks follow that frame.

trend: Assessed mainly as project work, but the consumer's rights, the three-tier machinery under COPRA and the duties of a consumer recur as 3-mark questions.
onepager: - A consumer is exploited because traders are organised and consumers are scattered and small.
- COPRA 1986 (24 December = National Consumers' Day); District, State and National Commissions.
- Six rights: informed, choose, redressal, represent, safety, education.
- ISI = industrial goods, Agmark = agricultural produce, Hallmark = gold and silver purity.
- Always take a cash memo — it is the proof needed to file a complaint.
task: Visit one shop near your home and record: the MRP and actual price charged on three items, whether a bill was given, and whether any item carried an ISI or Agmark mark. Write it up as a one-page consumer survey with a photograph — that is a complete internal assessment project.
